claim: The co-crystal structure of the PRPP aptamer and its ligand was determined at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: Here we report the co-crystal structure of the PRPP aptamer and its ligand.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the structure was determined and provides crystallographic data in Supplementary file 1 showing 2.5 Å resolution.

claim: The G96A point mutant prefers ppGpp over PRPP with a 40,000-fold switch in specificity.
source: We also report the structure of the G96A point mutant that prefers ppGpp over PRPP with a dramatic 40,000-fold switch in specificity.
evidence: The manuscript provides binding data in Table 1 showing Kd values that support this calculated fold change.

claim: The ends of the PRPP aptamer form a helix (P0) that is not present in the guanidine aptamer.
source: The ends of the aptamer form a helix that is not present in the guanidine aptamer and is involved in the expression platform.
evidence: The crystal structure shows P0 helix formation, and comparison with guanidine aptamer structure confirms its absence there.

claim: In the G96A mutant, the base of ppGpp replaces G96 in three-dimensional space.
source: In the mutant, the base of ppGpp replaces G96 in three-dimensional space.
evidence: Structural overlay data and Figure 6A demonstrate this spatial replacement.

claim: The G96A mutation disrupts the S-turn motif, which is a primary structural feature of the ykkC RNA motif.
source: This disrupts the S-turn, which is a primary structural feature of the ykkC RNA motif.
evidence: Structural comparison shows loss of S-turn characteristics in the mutant structure.

claim: ykkC aptamers are an example of an RNA fold with a rugged fitness landscape.
source: ykkC aptamers are therefore a prime example of an RNA fold with a rugged fitness landscape.
evidence: The dramatic specificity changes with minimal mutations support this interpretation.

claim: The ykkC aptamer's ability to acquire new specificity represents a striking case of evolvability in RNA.
source: The ease with which the ykkC aptamer acquires new specificity represents a striking case of evolvability in RNA.
evidence: The single point mutation causing 40,000-fold specificity switch demonstrates evolvability.

claim: RNA has diverse functional capabilities.
source: RNA has diverse functional capabilities, which has driven speculation that the first organisms may have been RNA-based (Breaker, 2012; Crick, 1968; Gilbert, 1986; Orgel, 2004; 1968; Strobel, 2001; Woese et al., 1966).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on RNA capabilities.

claim: For the RNA world hypothesis to be plausible, RNA must be adaptable and capable of acquiring new functions through mutation.
source: For this hypothesis to be plausible, RNA must be adaptable; that is, capable of acquiring new functions through mutation.
evidence: This is a logical requirement derived from the RNA world hypothesis.

claim: Evolvability is the propensity of a system to produce a mutated genotype that yields a beneficial phenotype under new selective pressures.
source: Evolvability is the propensity of a system to produce a mutated genotype that yields a beneficial phenotype under new selective pressures (Ancel and Fontana, 2000; Kirschner and Gerhart, 1998; Wagner, 2008; Wagner and Altenberg, 1996).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to evolutionary biology literature.

claim: Bacterial β-lactamases demonstrate significant evolvability through mutations in the Ω-loop.
source: For example, bacterial β-lactamases demonstrate significant evolvability through mutations in the Ω-loop. This loop determines substrate specificity, but mutation or outright deletion of the loop does not dramatically affect the overall structure of the protein (Banerjee et al., 1998; Hujer et al., 2001; Kurokawa et al., 2000; Wachino et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on β-lactamases.

claim: The ykkC RNA motif was discovered in 2004.
source: The ykkC RNA was discovered in 2004 and its ligand(s) remained unknown for over a decade (Barrick et al., 2004; Nelson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barrick et al., 2004.

claim: The ligand(s) of ykkC RNA remained unknown for over a decade after its discovery.
source: The ykkC RNA was discovered in 2004 and its ligand(s) remained unknown for over a decade (Barrick et al., 2004; Nelson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing discovery in 2004 and ligand identification in 2017.

claim: In 2017, Nelson et al. discovered that the majority of ykkC RNAs bind specifically to the guanidinium cation.
source: In 2017, Nelson et al. published two pivotal discoveries regarding this motif: (1) the majority of these RNAs bind specifically to the guanidinium cation and (2) the ykkC riboswitch class can be divided into at least two subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nelson et al., 2017.

claim: The ykkC riboswitch class can be divided into at least two subtypes.
source: In 2017, Nelson et al. published two pivotal discoveries regarding this motif: (1) the majority of these RNAs bind specifically to the guanidinium cation and (2) the ykkC riboswitch class can be divided into at least two subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nelson et al., 2017.

claim: Subtype 1 ykkC RNA has approximately 1500 known examples and is now known as the guanidine-I riboswitch.
source: Subtype 1, which has approximately 1500 known examples, is the major class now known as the guanidine-I riboswitch.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis cited from Nelson et al., 2017.

claim: Subtype 2 ykkC variants retain the same overall fold as guanidine-I but possess key differences at nucleotides crucial for guanidine binding.
source: The subtype 2 variants are overall quite similar to guanidine-I riboswitches. They retain the same overall fold, but possess a few characteristic differences at nucleotides crucial for guanidine binding.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural comparisons.

claim: Most differences between subtype 1 and 2 are centered around a classic S-turn motif that forms the binding pocket of the guanidine-I riboswitch.
source: Notably, most of these differences are centered around a classic S-turn motif that forms the binding pocket of the guanidine-I riboswitch.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison.

claim: Where guanidine riboswitches have a conserved adenosine residue (A46), subtypes 2a and 2b have a pyrimidine (C49).
source: For example, where guanidine riboswitches have a conserved adenosine residue (A46 in the guanidine-I structure solved by Reiss et al.), subtypes 2a and 2b have a pyrimidine (C49 in the present study) (Battaglia et al., 2017; Reiss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural data.

claim: Sorting the entire ykkC class by the identity of position 46/49 results in a strikingly complete segregation of guanidine-related gene contexts from those that are incongruent with mitigation of guanidine toxicity.
source: Sorting the entire ykkC class by the identity of this position alone results in a strikingly complete segregation of guanidine-related gene contexts from those that are incongruent with mitigation of guanidine toxicity (Nelson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis cited from Nelson et al., 2017.

claim: Subtype 2a and 2b ykkC riboswitches do not retain the ligand specificity of their parent riboswitch.
source: Subtype 2a and 2b ykkC riboswitches do not retain the ligand specificity of their parent riboswitch.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Sherlock et al. showing no response to guanidine.

claim: Subtype 2a ykkC riboswitch is responsive to guanosine tetra/pentaphosphate (ppGpp).
source: Instead, subtype 2a is responsive to guanosine tetra/pentaphosphate ((p)ppGpp, hereafter referred to as ppGpp), an alarmone that regulates the stringent response (Cashel and Gallant, 1969; Dalebroux and Swanson, 2012; Gaca et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on transcription termination and in-line probing assays from Sherlock et al., 2018a.

claim: Subtype 2b ykkC riboswitch is responsive to phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP).
source: Subtype 2b is responsive to phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP), a precursor in purine biosynthesis.
evidence: This is based on experimental assays from Sherlock et al., 2018b.

claim: Both subtype 2a and 2b ykkC riboswitches function as ON switches.
source: Like the guanidine riboswitch, both function as ON switches.
evidence: This is based on functional characterization from Sherlock et al.

claim: The most apparent difference between subtypes 2a and 2b is a highly-conserved guanosine (G96) in subtype 2b that is not conserved in subtype 2a.
source: The most apparent difference is a highly-conserved guanosine (G96 in this study) in subtype 2b that is not conserved in subtype 2a.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and bioinformatic analysis.

claim: G96 is equivalent to G89 in the guanidine-I riboswitch and is a conserved part of its S-turn motif.
source: This residue is equivalent to G89 in the guanidine-I riboswitch and is a conserved part of its S-turn motif.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment with the guanidine-I riboswitch structure.

claim: PRPP is an activated form of ribose 5-phosphate and a major macromolecular building block.
source: PRPP is an activated form of ribose 5-phosphate, and a major macromolecular building block (Hove-Jensen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PRPP is a central metabolite used in biosynthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, the amino acids histidine and tryptophan, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, thiamine diphosphate, flavins, and pterins.
source: It is a central metabolite used in biosynthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, the amino acids histidine and tryptophan, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, thiamine diphosphate, flavins, and pterins (Hove-Jensen, 1988; Jiménez et al., 2008; White, 1996).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ppGpp is an alarmone that initiates the stringent response, a global reaction to nutrient starvation in bacteria.
source: ppGpp is an alarmone that initiates the stringent response, a global reaction to nutrient starvation in bacteria (Cashel and Gallant, 1969; Cashel and Kalbacher, 1970; O'Farrell, 1978; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Amino acid starvation triggers synthesis of ppGpp.
source: Amino acid starvation triggers synthesis of ppGpp and it binds to a variety of effector molecules to initiate sweeping changes in the cell's transcriptional profile, including a reduction in tRNA and rRNA synthesis and an increase in transcription of amino acid biosynthesis genes (Cashel, 1970; Paul et al., 2005; Ryals et al., 1982; van Ooyen et al., 1976).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ppGpp riboswitch turns on transcription of amino acid biosynthesis and transport genes in response to alarmone binding.
source: Consistent with a role in the stringent response, the ppGpp riboswitch turns on transcription of amino acid biosynthesis and transport genes in response to alarmone binding.
evidence: This is based on gene context analysis and functional studies.

claim: A common ancestral RNA likely diverged to recognize guanidine, PRPP, and ppGpp.
source: Although the tree topology is unknown, a common ancestral RNA likely diverged to recognize guanidine, PRPP, and ppGpp in spite of the chemical and structural diversity among these ligands.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and sequence similarities among the aptamers.

claim: PRPP and ppGpp are more similar to each other than either is to guanidine.
source: PRPP and ppGpp are more similar to each other than either is to guanidine, which reflects the greater similarity in their aptamers.
evidence: This is based on chemical structure comparison and sequence similarity of aptamers.

claim: Guanidine harbors a single delocalized positive charge.
source: While guanidine harbors a single delocalized positive charge, PRPP and ppGpp harbor multiple separate loci of negative charge.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: PRPP and ppGpp harbor multiple separate loci of negative charge.
source: While guanidine harbors a single delocalized positive charge, PRPP and ppGpp harbor multiple separate loci of negative charge.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: Guanidine is small and achiral with three-fold rotational symmetry.
source: Guanidine is small and achiral with three-fold rotational symmetry, while PRPP and ppGpp are larger, chiral, asymmetric molecules.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: PRPP and ppGpp are larger, chiral, asymmetric molecules.
source: Guanidine is small and achiral with three-fold rotational symmetry, while PRPP and ppGpp are larger, chiral, asymmetric molecules.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: PRPP and ppGpp both contain ribose sugars and pyrophosphate moieties.
source: PRPP and ppGpp both contain ribose sugars and pyrophosphate moieties, but ppGpp has an entire guanine base that PRPP lacks.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: ppGpp has an entire guanine base that PRPP lacks.
source: PRPP and ppGpp both contain ribose sugars and pyrophosphate moieties, but ppGpp has an entire guanine base that PRPP lacks.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: The crystal structure of the wild-type PRPP aptamer was determined at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: To understand the basis of ligand recognition by the PRPP riboswitch, we determined the crystal structure of the aptamer domain of the ykkC 2b riboswitch from Thermoanaerobacter mathranii at 2.5 Å resolution in the presence of its native ligand, PRPP (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Crystallographic data are provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: PRPP is an activated metabolic intermediate that is highly unstable.
source: PRPP is an activated metabolic intermediate. As a result, it is highly unstable.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PRPP degrades on a time course of minutes to hours via several mechanisms in the presence of divalent metal ions, acidic or basic pH, and/or elevated temperatures.
source: It degrades on a time course of minutes to hours via several mechanisms in the presence of divalent metal ions, acidic or basic pH, and/or elevated temperatures (Dennis et al., 2000; Hove-Jensen et al., 2017; Khorana et al., 1958; 1955; Meola et al., 2003; Remy et al., 1955).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on PRPP stability.

claim: Binding to the PRPP riboswitch aptamer domain protects PRPP on a time scale of hours to days.
source: However, binding to the PRPP riboswitch aptamer domain protects PRPP on a time scale of hours to days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structure of the wild-type PRPP aptamer was solved by molecular replacement using the guanidine-I aptamer as an initial model.
source: The structure was solved by molecular replacement using the guanidine-I aptamer as an initial model.
evidence: This is a standard crystallographic method described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The wild-type PRPP aptamer structure was refined to an Rwork of 0.216 and an Rfree of 0.253.
source: After model building and refinement, the model fit the data with an Rwork of 0.216 and an Rfree of 0.253.
evidence: These are crystallographic refinement statistics.

claim: Like its parent aptamer, the PRPP riboswitch contains two adjacent helical stacks.
source: Like its parent aptamer, the PRPP riboswitch contains two adjacent helical stacks (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 1.

claim: P3 forms a large portion of the binding pocket in the PRPP aptamer.
source: P3 forms a large portion of the binding pocket, and a conserved loop at the end of P3 docks into P1a.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A conserved loop at the end of P3 docks into P1a in the PRPP aptamer.
source: P3 forms a large portion of the binding pocket, and a conserved loop at the end of P3 docks into P1a.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Conserved nucleotides from P1a participate in ligand recognition in the PRPP aptamer.
source: This allows conserved nucleotides from P1a to participate in ligand recognition.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing contacts between P1a nucleotides and PRPP.

claim: P1, P1a, P1b, and P2 together form a continuous coaxial stack adjacent to P3 in the PRPP aptamer.
source: P1, P1a, P1b, and P2 together form a continuous coaxial stack adjacent to P3.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The PRPP aptamer has structured tails at the 5′ and 3′ ends that are not conserved in the guanidine riboswitch.
source: However, unlike the guanidine aptamer, the PRPP aptamer has structured tails at the 5′ and 3′ ends that are not conserved in the guanidine riboswitch.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the PRPP structure with the guanidine structure and consensus sequences.

claim: The ends of the PRPP aptamer pair to form an additional short helix termed P0.
source: The ends pair to form an additional short helix that we have termed P0, resulting in a four-way junction between P0, P1, P2, and P3.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: P0 coaxially stacks with P3 in the PRPP aptamer.
source: P0 coaxially stacks with P3 and extends the binding pocket for recognition of the larger PRPP ligand.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: P0 extends the binding pocket for recognition of the larger PRPP ligand.
source: P0 coaxially stacks with P3 and extends the binding pocket for recognition of the larger PRPP ligand.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing P0 nucleotides contacting PRPP.

claim: PRPP is modeled with an occupancy of 1 in the crystal structure.
source: PRPP is modeled with an occupancy of 1, and its B factors refined similarly to those of nearby residues.
evidence: This is a crystallographic modeling parameter.

claim: PRPP is known to interact with two divalent metal ions per molecule in solution.
source: PRPP is known to interact with two divalent metal ions per molecule in solution. The 5-phosphate associates weakly with one metal and the pyrophosphate moiety more strongly coordinates a second metal (Thompson et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the PRPP riboswitch complex, two metal ions are present coordinating PRPP.
source: In the current model, these two metals are present in the complex with the riboswitch (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: One metal (M1) associates with the 5-phosphate of PRPP in the riboswitch complex.
source: One metal (M1) associates with the 5-phosphate, and the second metal (M2) associates with the pyrophosphate.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A second metal (M2) associates with the pyrophosphate of PRPP in the riboswitch complex.
source: One metal (M1) associates with the 5-phosphate, and the second metal (M2) associates with the pyrophosphate.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Both M1 and M2 form contacts bridging PRPP and the RNA aptamer.
source: Both metals form contacts bridging PRPP and the RNA aptamer.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A third metal ion (M3) forms a water-mediated coordination to the 5-phosphate of PRPP.
source: A third metal ion, M3, forms a water-mediated coordination to the 5-phosphate.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The three phosphate groups of PRPP are major elements of recognition via interactions with nucleobase amines and divalent metal ions.
source: The three phosphate groups are major elements of recognition via interactions with nucleobase amines and divalent metal ions.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing multiple contacts.

claim: The PRPP aptamer construct crystallizes in the presence of BaCl2.
source: This construct crystallizes in the presence of BaCl2, so both Ba2+ and Mg2+ are present in the crystallization condition.
evidence: This is stated in the crystallization conditions.

claim: M1 and M3 are modeled as Ba2+ due to the appearance of large positive peaks in the electron density map when modeled as Mg2+.
source: M1 and M3 are modeled as Ba2+ due to the appearance of large positive peaks in the electron density map when they are modeled as Mg2+.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic electron density analysis.

claim: M2 is modeled as Mg2+ but exhibits coordination distances higher than expected for this species.
source: M2 is modeled as Mg2+, but exhibits coordination distances higher than expected for this species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on crystallographic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The aptamer binds PRPP with nearly equal affinity in the presence of either Ba2+ or Mg2+ alone (2.0 ± 0.4 and 2.0 ± 0.3 µM, respectively).
source: The aptamer binds PRPP with nearly equal affinity in the presence of either Ba2+ or Mg2+ alone (2.0 ± 0.4 and 2.0 ± 0.3 µM, respectively).
evidence: This is based on equilibrium dialysis binding experiments.

claim: The N1 and N2 of G48 form hydrogen bonds with two phosphate oxygens of the 5-phosphate of PRPP.
source: The N1 and N2 of G48 form hydrogen bonds with two phosphate oxygens, while the N4 of C78 hydrogen bonds to the third non-bridging phosphate oxygen.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The N4 of C78 hydrogen bonds to a non-bridging phosphate oxygen of the 5-phosphate of PRPP.
source: The N1 and N2 of G48 form hydrogen bonds with two phosphate oxygens, while the N4 of C78 hydrogen bonds to the third non-bridging phosphate oxygen.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The 5-phosphate of PRPP coordinates M1.
source: The 5-phosphate also coordinates M1, which is held in place by coordination interactions with a non-bridging phosphate oxygen of C77 and the O2 of C49.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The residue equivalent to C49 is conserved as an adenosine in the guanidine-I riboswitch but is a pyrimidine in PRPP and ppGpp riboswitches.
source: The residue equivalent to C49 is conserved as an adenosine in the guanidine-I riboswitch but is a pyrimidine in PRPP and ppGpp riboswitches, and the identity of residue 49 was used as a marker to distinguish between these two variants (Sherlock et al., 2018a; 2018b).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The ribose moiety of PRPP makes extensive interactions with the RNA aptamer.
source: The ribose moiety of PRPP also makes extensive interactions with the RNA aptamer (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The sugar edge of G96 forms hydrogen bonds with the 2- and 3-hydroxyl groups of the PRPP ribose.
source: The sugar edge of G96 forms hydrogen bonds with the 2- and 3-hydroxyl groups.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The N4 of C77 donates a hydrogen bond to the ribose oxygen of PRPP.
source: The N4 of C77 donates a hydrogen bond to the ribose oxygen, and the N1 group of G104 donates a hydrogen bond to the 2-hydroxyl group.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The N1 group of G104 donates a hydrogen bond to the 2-hydroxyl group of the PRPP ribose.
source: The N4 of C77 donates a hydrogen bond to the ribose oxygen, and the N1 group of G104 donates a hydrogen bond to the 2-hydroxyl group.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: G96, C77, and G104 are all highly conserved in the consensus sequence of the PRPP aptamer.
source: These three residues are all highly conserved in the consensus sequence of this aptamer.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the consensus sequence.

claim: A C2-endo pucker is the most likely conformation for the PRPP ribose in the complex.
source: At 2.5 Å resolution, conclusive determination of the sugar pucker is not possible, but a C2-endo pucker is the most likely conformation in this complex and it fits the electron density data well.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic modeling and chemical reasoning.

claim: The C2-endo conformation avoids a steric clash between the 2-hydroxyl and the β-phosphate of PRPP.
source: This conformation avoids a steric clash between the 2-hydroxyl and the β-phosphate and allows the 3-hydroxyl to coordinate M2.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The C2-endo conformation is consistent with previously reported structures of PRPP in complex with macromolecules.
source: This conformation is also consistent with previously reported structures of PRPP in complex with macromolecules (Evans et al., 2014; González-Segura et al., 2007; Héroux et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other PRPP-containing structures.

claim: The P0 region of the aptamer extends below P3 and permits a suite of interactions with the pyrophosphate group of PRPP.
source: The P0 region of the aptamer extends below P3 and permits a suite of interactions with the pyrophosphate group of PRPP (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The β-phosphate of PRPP is more extensively recognized than the α-phosphate.
source: The β-phosphate of PRPP is more extensively recognized than the α-phosphate.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing more contacts to the β-phosphate.

claim: The O6 of G6 coordinates M2.
source: The O6 of G6 coordinates M2, which in turn forms several interactions with the pyrophosphate group (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The N6 group of A101 contacts a non-bridging oxygen of the α-phosphate of PRPP.
source: The N6 group of the weakly conserved A101 (>75% conserved as a purine) contacts a non-bridging oxygen of the α-phosphate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The N6 group of A5 and the N1 groups of G6 and G105 make direct contacts with non-bridging oxygens of the β-phosphate of PRPP.
source: The N6 group of A5 and the N1 groups of G6 and G105 make direct contacts with non-bridging oxygens of the β-phosphate.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A lone pair-π interaction forms between the O6 atom of G105 and the six-membered ring of A103.
source: An abrupt deformation in the local backbone conformation positions A103 under G105, allowing a lone pair-π interaction to form between the O6 atom of G105 and the six-membered ring of A103 (Chawla et al., 2017; Egli and Sarkhel, 2007; Ran and Hobza, 2009; Sarkhel and Desiraju, 2003; Singh and Das, 2015).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and supported by citations on lone pair-π interactions.

claim: The intracellular PRPP concentration in bacteria is estimated to be in the millimolar range.
source: The intracellular PRPP concentration in bacteria is estimated to be in the millimolar range (Hove-Jensen et al., 2017; Jendresen et al., 2011; Jensen et al., 1979; Nygaard and Smith, 1993; Saxild and Nygaard, 1991; Schneider and Gourse, 2004; Yaginuma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on multiple citations to studies measuring intracellular PRPP concentrations.

claim: Enzymes and protein regulatory elements that sense PRPP concentrations in bacteria typically have micromolar dissociation (Kd) or Michaelis (KM) constants.
source: However, enzymes and protein regulatory elements that sense PRPP concentrations in bacteria typically have micromolar dissociation (Kd) or Michaelis (KM) constants (Bera et al., 2003; Hove-Jensen et al., 2017; Jørgensen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on citations to studies of PRPP-binding proteins.

claim: The T50 of a PRPP riboswitch in transcription termination assays is 90 μM.
source: Sherlock and colleagues recently found that the T50 (the ligand concentration that produces half-maximal effect) of a PRPP riboswitch in transcription termination assays is 90 μM (Sherlock et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is based on citation to Sherlock et al., 2018b.

claim: The Kd of the PRPP riboswitch aptamer domain for PRPP is 2.0 ± 0.3 μM.
source: We determined the Kd of the riboswitch aptamer domain for PRPP (Table 1, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) by equilibrium dialysis using radiolabeled [β-33P]-PRPP. This assay yields a Kd of 2.0 ± 0.3 μM.
evidence: This is based on equilibrium dialysis experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The G96A mutant binds ppGpp with an affinity equivalent to that of wild-type for PRPP (Kd = 1.8 ± 0.1 μM).
source: Conversely, the G96A mutant binds ppGpp with an affinity equivalent to that of wild-type for PRPP (Kd = 1.8 ± 0.1 μM), but PRPP binding is abolished in the mutant up to 400 μM RNA (estimated Kd = 1600 ± 200 μM).
evidence: This is based on equilibrium dialysis experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: PRPP binding is abolished in the G96A mutant up to 400 μM RNA (estimated Kd = 1600 ± 200 μM).
source: Conversely, the G96A mutant binds ppGpp with an affinity equivalent to that of wild-type for PRPP (Kd = 1.8 ± 0.1 μM), but PRPP binding is abolished in the mutant up to 400 μM RNA (estimated Kd = 1600 ± 200 μM).
evidence: This is based on equilibrium dialysis experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: The G96A mutant has approximately 900-fold higher affinity for ppGpp than PRPP.
source: The G96A mutant has approximately 900-fold higher affinity for ppGpp than PRPP.
evidence: This is calculated from the Kd values in Table 1.

claim: The wild-type aptamer shows low affinity for ppGpp (Kd = 91 ± 3 μM) and 46-fold greater affinity for PRPP (Kd = 2.0 ± 0.3 μM).
source: The wild-type aptamer shows low affinity for ppGpp (Kd = 91 ± 3 μM) and 46-fold greater affinity for PRPP (Kd = 2.0 ± 0.3 μM) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on equilibrium dialysis experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: The crystal structure of the G96A mutant was solved to 3.1 Å resolution in the presence of ppGpp.
source: Having shown that the G96A mutant is a ppGpp aptamer, we solved its crystal structure in the presence of ppGpp to 3.1 Å resolution.
evidence: Crystallographic data are provided in the manuscript.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the G96A mutant crystal contained four aptamer molecules.
source: The asymmetric unit contained four aptamer molecules.
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation.

claim: The quality of the electron density was worse in chain D compared to chains A-C in the G96A mutant structure.
source: Molecular replacement and refinement revealed robust density for the electron-dense pyrophosphate groups of ppGpp as well as its guanine base. In the initial solution and throughout refinement, the quality of the electron density was worse in chain D compared to chains A-C.
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation.

claim: The overall architecture of the G96A mutant is very similar to that of the wild-type aptamer.
source: Overall, the architecture of the G96A mutant is very similar to that of the wild-type aptamer (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The G96A mutation caused major conformational rearrangement in the region around position 96.
source: Notably, the 2FO−FC map generated directly by molecular replacement showed no electron density in the former location of the ribose and phosphate of G96. Additional lack of electron density for the ribose of G95 and the phosphate of G97 immediately suggested that the G96A mutation caused major conformational rearrangement in this region.
evidence: This is based on electron density analysis during structure determination.

claim: The 5′ pyrophosphate of ppGpp occupies the former position of the pyrophosphate of PRPP.
source: The positions of the 5′ and 3′ pyrophosphate groups of ppGpp are easily inferred from the available electron density data, which clearly show that the 5′ pyrophosphate occupies the former position of the pyrophosphate of PRPP.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the PRPP and ppGpp structures.

claim: The ppGpp ribose has the opposite orientation of the PRPP ribose.
source: This results in the ppGpp ribose having the opposite orientation of the PRPP ribose.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures.

claim: The 5′ pyrophosphate is oriented toward P0 in the ppGpp structure, but the 5-phosphate is oriented away from P0 in the PRPP structure.
source: The 5′ pyrophosphate is oriented toward P0 in the ppGpp structure, but the 5-phosphate is oriented away from P0 in the PRPP structure (Figure 1C,D, 2A and 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in the cited figures.

claim: Several metal ions appear to associate with the pyrophosphate moieties of ppGpp.
source: Several metal ions appear to associate with the pyrophosphate moieties.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The positioning of metal ions is highly variable among the molecules in the asymmetric unit of the G96A structure.
source: The positioning of these entities is highly variable among the molecules in the asymmetric unit, suggesting that they do not make essential contributions to ligand recognition, but may provide general charge stabilization.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The guanine base of ppGpp is modeled in the syn conformation.
source: The guanine base of ppGpp is modeled in the syn conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on crystallographic modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The shape of the electron density appears visibly more consistent with the syn conformation than the anti conformation for ppGpp.
source: The shape of the electron density appears visibly more consistent with the syn conformation than the anti conformation.
evidence: This is based on electron density analysis.

claim: In the syn conformation, the guanine base of ppGpp forms three hydrogen bonds with C75 in a Watson-Crick base pair.
source: In the syn conformation, the guanine base of the ligand forms three hydrogen bonds with C75 in a Watson-Crick base pair.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: In the anti conformation, the Hoogsteen face of the guanine base would form just one hydrogen bond with the Watson-Crick face of C75.
source: In the anti conformation, the Hoogsteen face of the guanine base would form just one hydrogen bond with the Watson-Crick face of C75.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling.

claim: A C75U mutant in a native ppGpp riboswitch confers specificity to adenine-containing ligands over guanine-containing ligands.
source: Modeling a Watson-Crick base pair (syn conformation) is consistent with a recent study showing that the equivalent of a C75U mutant in a native ppGpp riboswitch confers specificity to adenine-containing ligands over guanine-containing ligands (Sherlock et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is based on citation to Sherlock et al., 2018a.

claim: The syn conformation of ppGpp was previously observed in a 2.0 Å X-ray crystal structure of an E. coli lysine decarboxylase, LcdI.
source: The syn conformation of ppGpp was previously observed in a 2.0 Å X-ray crystal structure of an E. coli lysine decarboxylase, LcdI (Kanjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on citation to Kanjee et al., 2011.

claim: In the syn conformation, the base of ppGpp in the G96A structure occupies the same position as the base of G96 in the wild type structure.
source: Finally, a structural overlay of the wild-type and G96A structures at C75 shows that in the syn conformation, the base of ppGpp in the G96A structure occupies the same position as the base of G96 in the wild type structure.
evidence: This is observed in structural overlays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The 3′ pyrophosphate of ppGpp consistently sits in a pocket lined with hydrogen bond donors.
source: The 3′ pyrophosphate of ppGpp consistently sits in a pocket lined with hydrogen bond donors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The N4 of C77, the N1 and N2 of G48, and the 2′OH of A76 all make hydrogen bonds to the 3′ pyrophosphate oxygens of ppGpp.
source: The N4 of C77, the N1 and N2 of G48, and the 2′OH of A76 all make hydrogen bonds to the phosphate oxygens.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A76 and G48 form a type I A-minor-like interaction in which the Watson-Crick edge of G48 interacts with the ligand.
source: A76 and G48 form a type I A-minor-like interaction in which the Watson-Crick edge of G48 interacts with the ligand, rather than being involved in a canonical base pair.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The 3′ pyrophosphate of ppGpp occupies a slightly different position in each molecule of the asymmetric unit.
source: While the position of the 5′-pyrophosphate of ppGpp is relatively invariable, the 3′-pyrophosphate occupies a slightly different position in each molecule of the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The 3′ pyrophosphate atoms have slightly higher B factors than the rest of the ppGpp ligand.
source: Consistent with this model, the 3′ pyrophosphate atoms have slightly higher B factors than the rest of the ligand (~138 Å2 for the 3′ pyrophosphate compared to ~119 Å2 for the 5′ pyrophosphate).
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation.

claim: The guanine base of ppGpp is buried in the RNA and is the focal point of ligand recognition.
source: The guanine base of ppGpp is buried in the RNA and is the focal point of ligand recognition.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing extensive contacts.

claim: In the PRPP aptamer, C75 forms a Watson-Crick base pair with G96.
source: In the PRPP aptamer, the highly conserved C75 forms a Watson-Crick base pair with G96.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The G96A mutant ppGpp aptamer recognizes its ligand through a Watson-Crick base pair between the G of ppGpp and C75.
source: The G96A mutant ppGpp aptamer recognizes its ligand through a similar Watson-Crick base pair between the G of ppGpp and C75 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The guanine base of ppGpp is recognized via stacking with G6 and is 56% buried.
source: The guanine base of the ligand is also recognized via stacking with G6 and is 56% buried, compared to 38% of ppGpp overall.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The ribose of ppGpp is not recognized by the aptamer.
source: The ribose is not recognized by the aptamer, leaving the guanine base and pyrophosphates as the major points of recognition.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing no contacts to the ribose.

claim: Recognition of the 5′-pyrophosphate of ppGpp is extensive.
source: Recognition of the 5′-pyrophosphate of ppGpp is extensive; its phosphate oxygens accept several hydrogen bonds from amino groups of conserved nucleobases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 5′-α-phosphate of ppGpp appears to be unrecognized.
source: The 5′-α-phosphate appears to be unrecognized, consistent with its similar position to the poorly recognized α-phosphate of PRPP in the native structure.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Nucleotide A74 appears to play a conserved structural role in the PRPP and ppGpp aptamers.
source: Nucleotide A74 appears to play a conserved structural role in the PRPP and ppGpp aptamers.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and sequence conservation.

claim: In all three ykkC subtypes, A74 forms a noncanonical base pair with G6.
source: In all three ykkC subtypes it forms a noncanonical base pair with G6, which directly contacts PRPP and ppGpp, suggesting that it plays a role in positioning G6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the guanidine-I riboswitch, A6 flips out to form the same non-canonical base pair with A68 that is observed in the PRPP and ppGpp aptamers.
source: In the guanidine-I riboswitch, this nucleotide is not conserved. However, A6 in the guanidine-I crystal structure flips out to form the same non-canonical base pair with A68 (equivalent to A74) that is observed in the present study (Battaglia et al., 2017; Reiss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the guanidine-I structure.

claim: The guanidine-I and PRPP ykkC aptamers each have an S-turn motif in the P3 helix.
source: The guanidine-I and PRPP ykkC aptamers each have an S-turn motif in the P3 helix.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: In the guanidine-I aptamer, the orientation of G88 is reversed relative to its stacking partners and G89 flips out of the helix.
source: In the guanidine-I aptamer, the orientation of G88 is reversed relative to its stacking partners and G89 flips out of the helix. These are classic features of the S-turn.
evidence: This is observed in the guanidine-I crystal structure.

claim: The guanidine-I riboswitch possesses a cross-strand purine stack, a characteristic backbone kink on the opposite strand from the S-turn, and stabilizing hydrogen bonds.
source: The guanidine-I riboswitch also possesses a cross-strand purine stack, a characteristic backbone kink on the opposite strand from the S-turn, and stabilizing hydrogen bonds, all of which were first observed in the S-turn of the conserved sarcin-ricin loop in the 23S rRNA (Correll et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with the sarcin-ricin loop.

claim: In the PRPP riboswitch, G96 flips out and base pairs with C75 while also hydrogen bonding to PRPP.
source: In the PRPP riboswitch, a similar S-turn motif exists at the equivalent position (Figure 6B). Equivalent to G89 in guanidine-I, G96 flips out and base pairs with C75 while also hydrogen bonding to PRPP.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The cross-strand purine stack is absent in the PRPP riboswitch.
source: Notably, the cross-strand purine stack is absent in the PRPP riboswitch, but other S-turn characteristics are preserved.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the PRPP and guanidine-I structures.

claim: The S-turn motif is abolished in the G96A mutant.
source: Conversely, the S-turn motif is abolished in the G96A mutant, and no contacts are observed between A96 and other nucleotides.
evidence: This is observed in the G96A crystal structure.

claim: In the G96A mutant, G95 does not possess the reverse ribose orientation that defines an S-turn.
source: Even more significantly, G95 does not possess the reverse ribose orientation that defines an S-turn. Rather, this region resembles a standard A-form helix with a single nucleotide bulge.
evidence: This is observed in the G96A crystal structure.

claim: The guanine of ppGpp replaces the flipped out guanosine of the former S-turn motif (G89/G96).
source: The guanine of ppGpp replaces the flipped out guanosine of the former S-turn motif (G89/G96) (Figure 6), revealing that the S-turn is a key center of functional plasticity in the ykkC RNAs.
evidence: This is observed in structural overlays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The S-turn is a key center of functional plasticity in the ykkC RNAs.
source: The guanine of ppGpp replaces the flipped out guanosine of the former S-turn motif (G89/G96) (Figure 6), revealing that the S-turn is a key center of functional plasticity in the ykkC RNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes observed between wild-type and mutant.

claim: The mechanism of specificity switching is recruitment of C75 as a primary effector of ligand recognition.
source: Three-dimensional structural models of the wild type and G96A mutant aptamers reveal that the mechanism of specificity switching is recruitment of C75 as a primary effector of ligand recognition (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The presence or absence of the S-turn motif governs whether an RNA base or the ppGpp base can pair with C75.
source: The presence or absence of the S-turn motif governs whether an RNA base or the ppGpp base can pair with C75, and therefore controls the specificity of the aptamer.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences between wild-type and mutant.

claim: Metal M3 in the PRPP riboswitch binds in the location where the guanidine-I riboswitch binds guanidine.
source: The P0 region, which is not present in the guanidine-I riboswitch, recognizes a portion of the larger ligand; metal ion M3 binds in the location where its parent motif binds guanidine (Figure 6C; see also Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In an overlay of the S-turns of the sarcin-ricin loop, the guanidine-I riboswitch, and the PRPP riboswitch, the guanidino group of the bulged guanosine in the sarcin-ricin loop overlays almost exactly with the guanidinium cation.
source: In an overlay of the S-turns of the sarcin-ricin loop, the guanidine-I riboswitch, and the PRPP riboswitch, the guanidino group of the bulged guanosine in the sarcin-ricin loop overlays almost exactly with the guanidinium cation, and both roughly overlay with metal M3 in the PRPP riboswitch.
evidence: This is observed in structural overlays.

claim: The common binding site of M3 in the PRPP riboswitch and guanidine in the guanidine riboswitch may be a case of molecular exaptation.
source: The common binding site of M3 in the PRPP riboswitch and guanidine in the guanidine riboswitch may be a case of molecular exaptation (the co-option of an existing feature for a new purpose).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity of binding sites.

claim: The evolutionary relationship of the PRPP and guanidine aptamers remains uncertain.
source: However, the evolutionary relationship of these two aptamers remains uncertain.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current knowledge.

claim: The PRPP riboswitch is often found immediately downstream of a guanine riboswitch in an IMPLY two-input logic gate.
source: The present structural data shed additional light on the potential mechanism of switching in tandem guanine-PRPP aptamers (Sherlock et al., 2018b). The PRPP riboswitch (an ON switch), is often found immediately downstream of a guanine riboswitch (an OFF switch), in an IMPLY two-input logic gate (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and citation to Sherlock et al., 2018b.

claim: In tandem guanine-PRPP systems, transcription proceeds in all cases except when guanine is present and PRPP is not.
source: In these tandem systems, transcription proceeds in all cases except when guanine is present and PRPP is not.
evidence: This is based on the IMPLY logic gate behavior.

claim: PRPP binding disrupts formation of the guanine aptamer in tandem systems.
source: This suggests that PRPP binding disrupts formation of the guanine aptamer, allowing transcription to proceed when both ligands are present (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis.

claim: Formation of the P0 stem of the PRPP aptamer and the P1 stem of the guanine aptamer are mutually exclusive.
source: Its predicted secondary structure shows that formation of the P0 stem of the PRPP aptamer and the P1 stem of the guanine aptamer are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is based on secondary structure prediction.

claim: The 5′ tail of the PRPP aptamer participates in P0 and plays a central role in PRPP recognition.
source: The present data reveal that the 5′ tail of the PRPP aptamer participates in P0 and plays a central role in PRPP recognition.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: PRPP binding stabilizes P0 and disrupts the P1 helix of the guanine aptamer in the proposed model.
source: In the proposed model, PRPP binding stabilizes P0 and disrupts the P1 helix of the guanine aptamer.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis.

claim: The IMPLY character of the guanine-PRPP two-input gate may depend on the relative stabilities of the P0 and P1 helices.
source: The IMPLY character of this two-input gate may depend on the relative stabilities of the two helices, which in turn suggests that alternative logic gates could be constructed through mutation of P0 or P1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The ppGpp and T-box riboswitches are often found in tandem.
source: The ppGpp and T-box riboswitches are also often found in tandem.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: In the ppGpp/T-box tandem system, each riboswitch maintains its own expression platform.
source: In contrast with the PRPP/guanine tandem system, the ppGpp and T-box riboswitches each maintain their own expression platform, suggesting that they fold independently.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The independent folding of ppGpp and T-box riboswitches is consistent with the AND behavior of this logic gate.
source: This is consistent with the AND behavior of this logic gate and the unimportance of the order of the two aptamers within the molecular circuit, but future studies in vivo are needed to confirm this.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that requires further testing.

claim: The observed ability of the ykkC scaffold to reach new ligand specificities via mutation of a few key residues is reminiscent of other accounts of adaptability in both proteins and RNAs.
source: The observed ability of the ykkC scaffold to reach new ligand specificities via mutation of a few key residues is reminiscent of other accounts of adaptability in both proteins and RNAs.
evidence: This is a comparison with other known examples of evolvability.

claim: β-lactamases evolve to expand their catalytic repertoire through mutations in a flexible loop.
source: In a clinically relevant contemporary example, β-lactamases evolve to expand their catalytic repertoire through mutations in a flexible loop. These mutations preserve the overall architecture of the protein while enabling it to metabolize new variations on a common antibiotic scaffold, contributing to the worldwide threat of antibiotic resistance (Banerjee et al., 1998; Hujer et al., 2001; Kurokawa et al., 2000; Wachino et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on β-lactamases.

claim: The Tetrahymena ribozyme scaffold supports catalytic activities including self-cleavage, RNA polymerization, and peptide bond hydrolysis.
source: In a related RNA example, the Tetrahymena ribozyme scaffold supports catalytic activities including self-cleavage, RNA polymerization, and peptide bond hydrolysis, though this is likely due to the placement of the substrates into physical proximity with each other (Kruger et al., 1982; Lau and Ferré-D'Amaré, 2016; Piccirilli et al., 1992; Zaug and Cech, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the Tetrahymena ribozyme.

claim: Natural riboswitch aptamers subjected to directed evolution switch specificity but maintain their overall fold.
source: Natural riboswitch aptamers subjected to directed evolution switch specificity, but maintain their overall fold (Porter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Porter et al., 2017.

claim: The finding that a single conservative point mutation in the PRPP aptamer can dramatically alter both ligand specificity and tertiary structure reveals a striking example of RNA plasticity.
source: However, the present finding that a single conservative point mutation in the PRPP aptamer can dramatically alter both ligand specificity and tertiary structure reveals a striking example of RNA plasticity and speaks to the macromolecular evolvability of RNA.
evidence: This is based on the structural and biochemical data presented in the study.

claim: An RNA element has evolved to specifically recognize PRPP.
source: A final key observation in this study is the direct visualization that an RNA element has evolved to specifically recognize PRPP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure and binding data.

claim: PRPP is a central metabolite and likely has played that role since before the metabolic pathways of life's last universal common ancestor (LUCA) were fully developed.
source: PRPP is a central metabolite, and likely has played that role since before the metabolic pathways of life's last universal common ancestor (LUCA) were fully developed (Glansdorff et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glansdorff et al., 2008.

claim: It is possible that PRPP was used for the synthesis of nucleotide precursors on the prebiotic Earth.
source: It is possible that PRPP was used for the synthesis of nucleotide precursors on the prebiotic Earth (Akouche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akouche et al., 2017.

claim: The finding that an extant RNA specifically recognizes PRPP lends credence to the hypothesis that RNA elements may have been capable of recognizing PRPP before the advent of coded protein synthesis.
source: The finding that an extant RNA specifically recognizes PRPP lends credence to the hypothesis that RNA elements may have been capable of recognizing PRPP before the advent of coded protein synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discovery of the PRPP riboswitch.

claim: The wild type PRPP aptamer crystallized in space group P21 with two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: The wild type aptamer crystallized in space group P21 with two molecules present in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation.

claim: The G96A aptamer crystallized in space group P1 with four molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: The G96A aptamer crystallized in space group P1 with four molecules in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation.

claim: Coordinates have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with accession numbers 6CK5 for the wild-type PRPP aptamer and 6CK4 for the G96A ppGpp aptamer.
source: Coordinates have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with accession numbers 6CK5 for the wild-type PRPP aptamer and 6CK4 for the G96A ppGpp aptamer.
evidence: This is stated in the accession numbers section.
